# Why QR codes

A QR code is the only thing on a printed poster a reader can act on. It is
also the only way a two-minute conversation turns into a download.

Codes are generated from the URL at render time, so they cannot drift out of
sync with the link the way a pasted screenshot does, and they are vector — a
code stays sharp whether the poster prints at A2 or 48 inches wide.

# Placing a code

::: {.qr url="https://github.com/chrischizinski/quarto-sciposter" label="Source and documentation"}
:::

The `label` is optional but worth using: an unlabelled code asks the reader to
scan something without telling them what they get.

# Sizing

Default size is 2 inches. The practical floor is about 1.5 inches — below
that a phone struggles to lock on from a comfortable standing distance, and
the code becomes decoration rather than a link.

::: {.qr url="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.0000000" size="1.5in" label="Preprint (minimum usable size)"}
:::

Mount height matters as much as size. A code near the top of a mounted poster
can end up above head height, where nobody can hold a phone steady against it.
Keep codes in the lower two-thirds.

# Aligning against a neighbour

`offset` nudges a code down inside its cell; a negative value moves it up.

::: {.poster-grid cols="2" gutter="0.3in"}
::: {.qr url="https://example.org/left" size="1.5in" label="No offset"}
:::

::: {.qr url="https://example.org/right" size="1.5in" offset="0.25in" label="offset=\"0.25in\""}
:::
:::

Use it to pair a code with a logo whose transparent canvas defeats
`layout-valign`. Set it by eye — Typst cannot see where an image's ink starts.

# Notes

The QR package (`tiaoma`) is downloaded on first use and cached. A poster that
places no codes never fetches it.
